questions.q: 1 a) What is Point Estimation in Statistics?
questions.a: Point estimation is the technique of using a single numerical value, computed from sample data, to estimate an unknown population parameter. Formally an estimator is a statistic θ̂ = g(X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ), and the number it yields for the observed sample is the point estimate; for example x̄ = (1/n)·ΣXᵢ is the estimator of the population mean μ. Substituting the sample observations into the estimator gives one best-guess number rather than a range of plausible values. This contrasts with interval estimation, which produces a confidence interval. A good point estimator is unbiased (E[θ̂] = θ), consistent, efficient (minimum variance) and sufficient. Because a point estimate carries no built-in measure of uncertainty, it is usually reported together with its standard error.
steps: Identify the unknown population parameter θ to be estimated (for example the population mean μ).
Choose a sample statistic (the estimator) θ̂ = g(X₁,…,Xₙ), such as x̄ = (1/n)·ΣXᵢ for μ.
Substitute the observed sample data into the estimator to obtain a single numerical point estimate.
Assess the estimator using the criteria of unbiasedness E(θ̂) = θ, consistency, efficiency and sufficiency.
Report the point estimate; unlike a confidence interval it is a single number, so pair it with its standard error.
questions.formula: θ̂ = g(X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ); for a mean, x̄ = (1/n)·ΣXᵢ estimates μ
questions.explanation: Point estimation is defined by a single-number estimate derived from a sample, in contrast to interval estimation which supplies a confidence interval. The quality of an estimator is judged by unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency and sufficiency.
questions.oneShotPreview: A single sample-based number (estimator θ̂) used to estimate an unknown population parameter θ.

questions.q: 1 b) Find the value of correction factor if n=10 and N=1000.
questions.a: When sampling without replacement from a finite population, the finite population correction (FPC) factor is √[(N−n)/(N−1)]. Substituting N = 1000 and n = 10 gives √[(1000−10)/(1000−1)] = √(990/999) = √0.99099 ≈ 0.9955. The common approximation √(1−n/N) = √(1−10/1000) = √0.99 ≈ 0.995 gives essentially the same value. Since the sampling fraction n/N = 0.01 is small, the correction factor is close to 1 and is often ignored in large-sample work. Its role is to reduce the standard error relative to sampling with replacement.
steps: Recognise that the finite population correction (FPC) applies when sampling without replacement from a finite population.
State the formula: FPC = √[(N−n)/(N−1)].
Compute 990/999 ≈ 0.99099 and take the square root to get ≈ 0.9955 (approximation √0.99 ≈ 0.995).
Conclude that, because n/N = 0.01 is small, the factor is near 1 and is usually ignored.
questions.explanation: The FPC reduces the standard error when sampling without replacement from a finite population; substituting n = 10, N = 1000 gives √(990/999) ≈ 0.9955.

questions.q: 1 c) The variance of a population is 2. The size of the sample collected from the population is 169. What is the standard error of mean?
questions.a: The standard error of the sample mean is SE = σ/√n, where σ is the population standard deviation. Given the population variance σ² = 2, we have σ = √2 ≈ 1.4142. With sample size n = 169, √n = 13. Substituting into the formula gives SE = √2/13 ≈ 1.4142/13 ≈ 0.1088. Hence the standard error of the mean is about 0.109.
steps: Identify the required quantity: the standard error of the mean, SE = σ/√n.
From the given variance σ² = 2, obtain σ = √2 ≈ 1.4142.
With n = 169, compute √n = 13.
Substitute into the formula: SE = √2/13 ≈ 1.4142/13 ≈ 0.1088.
Conclude that the standard error of the mean is approximately 0.109.
questions.explanation: The standard error of the mean is σ/√n, so dividing √2 ≈ 1.4142 by 13 gives approximately 0.109.

questions.q: 1 d) Define Critical region.
questions.a: The critical region (or rejection region) is the set of values of a test statistic for which the null hypothesis H₀ is rejected. Its boundaries, called critical values, are fixed by the chosen significance level α and by whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed. For a two-tailed test the region occupies area α/2 in each tail, while for a one-tailed test it occupies area α in a single tail. If the computed statistic falls inside the critical region the result is statistically significant and H₀ is rejected; otherwise H₀ is not rejected. Thus the critical region is the formal rejection rule of the test.
steps: A hypothesis test partitions the sample space into a critical (rejection) region and an acceptance region.
The critical region is defined as the set of test-statistic values for which H₀ is rejected.
Its boundaries, the critical values, are fixed by the significance level α.
For a two-tailed test the region lies in both tails (area α/2 each); for a one-tailed test it lies in one tail (area α).
If the computed statistic lies in the critical region the result is significant and H₀ is rejected; otherwise H₀ is not rejected.
questions.formula: Reject H₀ if |Z| > Z_{α/2} (two-tailed) or Z > Z_α / Z < −Z_α (one-tailed)
questions.explanation: The critical region is precisely the rejection rule of a hypothesis test, determined by α and the tails of the sampling distribution.
questions.oneShotPreview: Set of test-statistic values that lead to rejecting H₀, fixed by α and the number of tails.

questions.q: 1 e) Define i) Null hypothesis ii) Alternative hypothesis.
questions.a: The null hypothesis (H₀) is a statement about a population parameter that is assumed true until sample evidence contradicts it; it represents the status quo or a no-difference / no-effect claim and is the hypothesis actually tested. It is stated with equality, for example H₀: μ = μ₀ or P = P₀. The alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) contradicts H₀ and is the competing statement the investigator seeks to establish, such as μ ≠ μ₀, μ > μ₀ or μ < μ₀. A test either rejects H₀ in favour of H₁, or fails to reject H₀; it never proves H₀. The alternative determines whether the test is two-tailed or one-tailed.
steps: A hypothesis test compares two competing statements about a population parameter θ.
The null hypothesis H₀ is the default no-effect / no-difference statement, assumed true until contradicted, and is the one tested; it is stated with equality (θ = θ₀).
The alternative hypothesis H₁ (or Hₐ) contradicts H₀ and is the claim the investigator wants to establish.
H₁ may be two-sided (θ ≠ θ₀) or one-sided (θ > θ₀ or θ < θ₀), which fixes the tails of the test.
The test either rejects H₀ in favour of H₁, or fails to reject H₀; it never establishes H₀ as proven.
questions.formula: H₀: θ = θ₀ versus H₁: θ ≠ θ₀ (two-tailed), θ > θ₀ or θ < θ₀ (one-tailed)
questions.explanation: H₀ is the default assumption being tested, while H₁ is the competing claim accepted only when H₀ is rejected; H₁ also decides the direction of the test.
questions.oneShotPreview: H₀ = default no-effect claim under test (equality); H₁ = competing claim we seek to establish.

questions.q: 2 a) A population consists of six numbers 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. Find the population mean.
questions.a: The population mean is defined as μ = ΣXᵢ/N, the sum of all population values divided by the population size. Here the population values are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, so N = 6. Their sum is 4 + 8 + 12 + 16 + 20 + 24 = 84. Substituting gives μ = 84/6 = 14. Therefore the population mean is 14.
steps: Identify the parameter: the population mean μ = ΣXᵢ/N.
List the population values 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 and note N = 6.
Substitute into the formula: μ = 84/6 = 14.
Conclude that the population mean is 14.
questions.explanation: The population mean is the sum of all population values divided by N = 6, giving 84/6 = 14.
questions.oneShotPreview: Population mean = 84/6 = 14.

questions.q: 2 b) A population consists of six numbers 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. Find the population standard deviation.
questions.a: The population variance is σ² = Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²/N and the standard deviation is its square root. Using μ = 14 from part (a), the deviations are −10, −6, −2, 2, 6, 10. Their squares are 100, 36, 4, 4, 36, 100, which sum to 280. Thus σ² = 280/6 ≈ 46.67 and σ = √(280/6) ≈ √46.67 ≈ 6.83. The population standard deviation is therefore about 6.83.
steps: State the parameter formulas: σ² = Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²/N and σ = √σ².
Use the population mean μ = 14 found earlier.
Compute deviations −10, −6, −2, 2, 6, 10 and their squares 100, 36, 4, 4, 36, 100.
Sum the squared deviations to get 280, so σ² = 280/6 ≈ 46.67.
Take the square root: σ = √(280/6) ≈ 6.83.
questions.explanation: Population standard deviation is √[Σ(X−μ)²/N]; dividing the sum of squared deviations 280 by N = 6 and taking the square root gives ≈ 6.83.

questions.q: 2 c) For samples of size two drawn without replacement from the population 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, find the mean of the sampling distribution of means.
questions.a: The mean of the sampling distribution of the sample mean is E(x̄) = μ_x̄, and a fundamental property of sampling distributions is that E(x̄) equals the population mean μ regardless of sample size or of whether sampling is with or without replacement. From part (a) the population mean of 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 is μ = 14. Therefore the average of all possible sample means of size two is μ_x̄ = 14. This equality holds exactly, so no enumeration is needed.
steps: Identify the parameter of interest: the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄, μ_x̄ = E(x̄).
Apply the sampling theorem E(x̄) = μ, valid for any sample size and with or without replacement.
Recall the population mean from part (a): μ = 14.
Substitute to obtain μ_x̄ = 14.
questions.explanation: By a fundamental property of sampling distributions, E(x̄) = μ, so the average of all possible sample means is 14 regardless of the sampling scheme.
questions.oneShotPreview: Mean of the sampling distribution of means = population mean = 14.

questions.q: 2 d) For samples of size two drawn without replacement from the population 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, find the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of means.
questions.a: For samples of size n drawn without replacement from a population of size N, the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean is σ_x̄ = (σ/√n)·√[(N−n)/(N−1)]. Here σ = √(280/6) ≈ 6.8313, n = 2 and N = 6. Thus σ/√n = 6.8313/√2 ≈ 4.8305 and the correction factor is √[(6−2)/(6−1)] = √(4/5) ≈ 0.8944, giving σ_x̄ ≈ 4.8305 × 0.8944 ≈ 4.32. Direct enumeration of all C(6,2) = 15 samples confirms this: the variance is (σ²/n)·[(N−n)/(N−1)] = (46.67/2)(0.8) ≈ 18.67, whose square root is ≈ 4.32.
steps: Identify the parameter: the standard error σ_x̄ = (σ/√n)·√[(N−n)/(N−1)] for sampling without replacement.
Verify by enumeration: variance = (280/6)/2 × 4/5 ≈ 18.67, so σ_x̄ = √18.67 ≈ 4.32.
questions.explanation: The without-replacement standard error formula and direct enumeration of the 15 sample means both give a standard deviation of about 4.32.
questions.oneShotPreview: Standard error of the mean ≈ 4.32 (n=2, N=6, without replacement).

questions.q: 3 A random sample of size 100 is taken from an infinite population having the mean μ = 76 and variance σ² = 256. What is the probability that x̄ will be between 75 and 78?
questions.a: By the central limit theorem the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ = 76 and standard error σ/√n. Here σ = √256 = 16 and n = 100, so SE = 16/10 = 1.6. Standardising the limits gives z₁ = (75−76)/1.6 = −0.625 and z₂ = (78−76)/1.6 = 1.25. Therefore P(75 < x̄ < 78) = Φ(1.25) − Φ(−0.625) = 0.8944 − 0.2660 = 0.6284. The probability is about 0.628, or 62.8%.
steps: By the CLT, x̄ is approximately N(μ, σ/√n) with μ = 76, σ² = 256 so σ = 16, and n = 100.
Compute the standard error: SE = σ/√n = 16/√100 = 16/10 = 1.6.
Standardise the limits: z₁ = (75−76)/1.6 = −0.625 and z₂ = (78−76)/1.6 = 1.25.
Conclude that the probability is approximately 0.6284 (62.8%).
questions.explanation: By the central limit theorem x̄ is approximately normal with mean 76 and SE 1.6; the area between z = −0.625 and z = 1.25 is about 0.628.

questions.q: 4 a) What is the maximum error one can expect to make with probability 0.9 when using the mean of a random sample of size n=64 to estimate the mean of a population with σ² = 2.56?
questions.a: The maximum error (margin of error) when estimating μ by x̄ is E = z_{α/2}·σ/√n. Here σ = √2.56 = 1.6 and n = 64, so the standard error is σ/√n = 1.6/8 = 0.2. A probability of 0.9 corresponds to 90% confidence, so α = 0.10 and z_{0.05} = 1.645. Substituting gives E = 1.645 × 0.2 = 0.329. Thus, with probability 0.9, the sample mean differs from the population mean by no more than about 0.33.
steps: Identify the quantity: the maximum error E when x̄ estimates the population mean μ.
State the formula E = z_{α/2}·σ/√n; for probability 0.90, z_{0.05} = 1.645.
From σ² = 2.56 obtain σ = 1.6, and with n = 64 compute SE = 1.6/8 = 0.2.
Conclude that with probability 0.9 the estimation error is at most about 0.33.
questions.explanation: The margin of error is z times the standard error; with z_{0.05} = 1.645 for 90% confidence and SE = 0.2, E ≈ 0.329.

questions.q: 4 b) A random sample of size 100 is taken from a population with σ = 5.1. Given that the sample mean is x̄ = 21.6, construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean μ.
questions.a: The large-sample 95% confidence interval for the population mean is x̄ ± z_{α/2}·σ/√n, with z_{0.025} = 1.96. Here n = 100, so the standard error is σ/√n = 5.1/10 = 0.51. The margin of error is 1.96 × 0.51 = 0.9996 ≈ 1.0. Hence the interval is 21.6 ± 0.9996, i.e. (20.6004, 22.5996). We are 95% confident that the true population mean lies between about 20.6 and 22.6.
steps: Identify the parameter to estimate: the population mean μ; the estimator is x̄ = 21.6.
State the formula CI = x̄ ± z_{α/2}·σ/√n with z_{0.025} = 1.96 for 95% confidence.
Compute the standard error: SE = σ/√n = 5.1/√100 = 0.51.
Compute the margin of error: 1.96 × 0.51 = 0.9996.
questions.explanation: A large-sample 95% confidence interval is x̄ ± z_{0.025}·σ/√n; substituting gives 21.6 ± 1.0, i.e. (20.60, 22.60).
questions.oneShotPreview: 95% confidence interval for μ ≈ (20.60, 22.60).

questions.q: 5 a) A sample of 400 items is taken from a population whose standard deviation is 10. The mean of the sample is 40. Test whether the sample has come from a population with mean 38.
questions.a: Set H₀: μ = 38 against H₁: μ ≠ 38, a two-tailed test. At α = 0.05 the critical values are Z_{0.025} = ±1.96 (and ±2.58 at 1%). The test statistic is Z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n); the standard error is 10/√400 = 10/20 = 0.5, so Z = (40 − 38)/0.5 = 4. Since |Z| = 4 exceeds 1.96 (and also 2.58), H₀ is rejected. The sample mean of 40 is significantly higher than 38, so the sample did not come from a population with mean 38.
steps: H₀: μ = 38 and H₁: μ ≠ 38 (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values Z_{0.025} = ±1.96 (also ±2.58 at the 1% level).
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since |Z| = 4 > 1.96, reject H₀.
Conclusion: the sample mean is significantly different from 38, so the sample is not from a population with mean 38.
questions.explanation: A large-sample z-test of the population mean gives z = 4, far beyond the 5% (1.96) and 1% (2.58) thresholds, so the claimed mean of 38 is untenable.
questions.oneShotPreview: z = 4 > 1.96; reject H₀ — sample is not from a mean-38 population.

questions.q: 5 b) In a random sample of 125 cool drinkers 68 said they prefer Thumsup to Pepsi. Test the null hypothesis P = 0.5 against the alternative hypothesis P > 0.5.
questions.a: We test H₀: P = 0.5 against H₁: P > 0.5, a right-tailed test at α = 0.05 with critical value Z_{0.05} = 1.645. The sample proportion is p̂ = 68/125 = 0.544 and the standard error under H₀ is √[P₀(1−P₀)/n] = √(0.5×0.5/125) = √0.002 ≈ 0.0447. Hence Z = (p̂ − P₀)/SE = (0.544 − 0.5)/0.0447 ≈ 0.98. Since 0.98 < 1.645, H₀ is not rejected. The data do not provide significant evidence that more than half of cool drinkers prefer Thumsup; the observed excess is attributable to sampling variation.
steps: H₀: P = 0.5 and H₁: P > 0.5 (right-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical value Z_{0.05} = 1.645.
Decision rule: reject H₀ if Z > 1.645; since 0.98 < 1.645, do not reject H₀.
Conclusion: there is no significant evidence that more than half prefer Thumsup.
questions.explanation: The one-sample proportion z-test gives z ≈ 0.98, below the one-tailed 5% cut-off of 1.645, so the observed excess is due to sampling variation.
questions.oneShotPreview: z ≈ 0.98 < 1.645; do not reject P = 0.5.

questions.q: 6 a) A sample of 64 students have mean weight of 70 kgs. Can this be regarded as a sample from a population with mean weight 56 kgs and standard deviation 25 kgs?
questions.a: Test H₀: μ = 56 against H₁: μ ≠ 56 at α = 0.05, with critical values ±1.96 (±2.58 at 1%). The test statistic is Z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n); the standard error is 25/√64 = 25/8 = 3.125, so Z = (70 − 56)/3.125 = 14/3.125 = 4.48. Since |Z| = 4.48 is far greater than 1.96 (indeed greater than 2.58), H₀ is rejected. The observed mean weight of 70 kg is incompatible with a population mean of 56 kg, so the sample cannot be regarded as drawn from that population.
steps: H₀: μ = 56 and H₁: μ ≠ 56 (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96 (also ±2.58 at 1%).
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since 4.48 > 1.96, reject H₀.
Conclusion: the sample with mean 70 kg cannot be regarded as coming from the population with mean 56 kg and σ = 25 kg.
questions.explanation: The z-statistic of 4.48 lies deep in the rejection region, showing the observed mean is incompatible with a population mean of 56 kg.
questions.oneShotPreview: z = 4.48 → reject; not a sample from the mean-56 population.

questions.q: 6 b) In a big city 325 men out of 600 men were found to be smokers. Does this information support the conclusion that the majority of men in this city are smokers?
questions.a: Test H₀: P = 0.5 against H₁: P > 0.5 (a majority), right-tailed at α = 0.05 with critical value 1.645. The sample proportion is p̂ = 325/600 ≈ 0.5417 and the standard error under H₀ is √[0.5×0.5/600] = √(0.25/600) ≈ 0.0204. Hence Z = (0.5417 − 0.5)/0.0204 ≈ 2.04. Since 2.04 > 1.645, H₀ is rejected at the 5% level, so the data support the majority claim; however 2.04 < 2.33, so the claim is not supported at the 1% level.
steps: H₀: P = 0.5 and H₁: P > 0.5 (a majority, right-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical value Z_{0.05} = 1.645 (at 1% it would be 2.33).
Decision rule: reject H₀ if Z > 1.645; since 2.04 > 1.645, reject at 5%, but 2.04 < 2.33 so not at 1%.
Conclusion: the information supports the conclusion that a majority of men are smokers at the 5% level.
questions.explanation: The one-tailed proportion test yields z ≈ 2.04, exceeding the 5% critical value 1.645 but below the 1% value 2.33, so the majority claim is supported at 5% only.
questions.oneShotPreview: z ≈ 2.04 > 1.645; yes, a majority are smokers at the 5% level.

questions.q: 7 The means of two large samples of sizes 1000 and 2000 members are 67.5 inches and 68.0 inches respectively. Can the samples be regarded as drawn from the same population of standard deviation 2.5 inches?
questions.a: Test H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ against H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ at α = 0.05 (critical values ±1.96). For two large samples with common σ = 2.5, the standard error of the difference is σ√[(1/n₁)+(1/n₂)] = 2.5√[(1/1000)+(1/2000)] = 2.5√0.0015 ≈ 0.0968. Thus Z = (68.0 − 67.5)/0.0968 = 0.5/0.0968 ≈ 5.16. Since |Z| = 5.16 > 1.96, H₀ is rejected. The samples cannot be regarded as drawn from the same population; the second sample mean is significantly higher.
steps: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ and H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96.
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since 5.16 > 1.96, reject H₀.
Conclusion: the samples are not drawn from the same population; the second sample mean is significantly larger.
questions.explanation: The two-sample z-test gives z ≈ 5.16, far beyond the 5% critical value, so the 0.5-inch difference cannot be attributed to chance.
questions.oneShotPreview: z ≈ 5.16 > 1.96; the samples come from different populations.

questions.q: 8 Samples of students were drawn from two universities and their weights in kilograms gave: University A — mean 55, S.D. 10, sample size 400; University B — mean 57, S.D. 15, sample size 100. Make a large sample test for the significance of the difference between the means.
questions.a: Test H₀: μ_A = μ_B against H₁: μ_A ≠ μ_B at α = 0.05 (critical values ±1.96). The standard error of the difference is √[(s_A²/n_A)+(s_B²/n_B)] = √(100/400 + 225/100) = √(0.25 + 2.25) = √2.5 ≈ 1.581. Hence Z = |57 − 55|/1.581 = 2/1.581 ≈ 1.26. Since 1.26 < 1.96, H₀ is not rejected. There is no statistically significant difference between the mean weights of the two universities; the 2 kg gap is within sampling error.
steps: H₀: μ_A = μ_B and H₁: μ_A ≠ μ_B (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96.
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since 1.26 < 1.96, do not reject H₀.
Conclusion: there is no significant difference between the mean weights of the two universities.
questions.explanation: The large-sample test for the difference of two means gives z ≈ 1.26, below the 5% critical value 1.96, so the 2 kg difference is within sampling error.
questions.oneShotPreview: z ≈ 1.26 < 1.96; no significant difference in mean weights.

questions.q: 9 In two large populations there are 30% and 25% respectively of fair haired people. Is this difference likely to be hidden in samples of 1200 and 900 respectively from the two populations?
questions.a: Test H₀: P₁ = P₂ against H₁: P₁ ≠ P₂ at α = 0.05 (critical values ±1.96). The pooled proportion is p = (0.30×1200 + 0.25×900)/(1200+900) = 585/2100 ≈ 0.2786, giving SE = √[p(1−p)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)] = √[0.2786×0.7214×(1/1200 + 1/900)] ≈ √0.000391 ≈ 0.0198. Hence Z = (0.30 − 0.25)/0.0198 = 0.05/0.0198 ≈ 2.53. Since 2.53 > 1.96, H₀ is rejected at the 5% level. The difference is statistically significant and therefore would not be hidden — samples of these sizes would reveal it.
steps: H₀: P₁ = P₂ and H₁: P₁ ≠ P₂ (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96.
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since 2.53 > 1.96, reject at 5%.
Conclusion: the difference is significant, so it is not likely to be hidden by samples of 1200 and 900.
questions.explanation: The two-proportion z-test gives z ≈ 2.53, exceeding 1.96, so the observed difference would be detected rather than concealed by these sample sizes.
questions.oneShotPreview: z ≈ 2.53 > 1.96; the difference is significant, not hidden.

questions.q: 10 a) An ambulance service claims that it takes on the average less than 10 minutes to reach its destination in emergency calls. A sample of 36 calls has a mean of 11 minutes and variance of 16 minutes. Test the significance at 0.05 level.
questions.a: The claim μ < 10 gives H₀: μ = 10 and H₁: μ < 10, a left-tailed test. At α = 0.05 the critical value is −1.645. With sample variance 16, s = 4 and the standard error is s/√n = 4/√36 = 4/6 ≈ 0.667. The test statistic is Z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) = (11 − 10)/0.667 = +1.5. Since +1.5 is not less than −1.645, it lies outside the rejection region and H₀ is not rejected. The sample does not support the claim of an average response below 10 minutes; the observed average is in fact 11 minutes.
steps: H₀: μ = 10 and H₁: μ < 10 (the claim, left-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical value −1.645.
Decision rule: reject H₀ only if Z < −1.645; since +1.5 is not in the rejection region, do not reject H₀.
Conclusion: the sample does not support the claim that the average response time is below 10 minutes.
questions.explanation: The claim requires a significantly small mean, but the sample mean of 11 minutes gives a positive z of 1.5, far from the left-tail cut-off of −1.645, so the claim cannot be accepted.
questions.oneShotPreview: z = +1.5 (not < −1.645); claim of mean < 10 minutes not supported.

questions.q: 10 b) Experience had shown that 20% of a manufactured product is of top quality. In one day's production of 400 articles only 50 are of top quality. Test the hypothesis at 0.05 level.
questions.a: Test H₀: P = 0.20 against H₁: P ≠ 0.20 at α = 0.05, with critical values ±1.96 (±2.58 at 1%). The observed proportion is p̂ = 50/400 = 0.125 and the standard error under H₀ is √[P₀(1−P₀)/n] = √(0.2×0.8/400) = √0.0004 = 0.02. Hence Z = (0.125 − 0.20)/0.02 = −0.075/0.02 = −3.75. Since |Z| = 3.75 > 1.96 (and > 2.58), H₀ is rejected. The day's production has a significantly lower proportion of top-quality articles than the expected 20%.
steps: H₀: P = 0.20 and H₁: P ≠ 0.20 (two-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical values ±1.96 (also ±2.58 at 1%).
Decision rule: reject H₀ if |Z| > 1.96; since 3.75 > 1.96, reject H₀ (also at 1%).
Conclusion: the top-quality rate is significantly lower than the expected 20%.

questions.q: 11 A sample of the heights of 6400 Englishmen has a mean of 67.85 inches and a standard deviation of 2.5 inches, while a sample of the heights of 1600 Australians has a mean of 68.55 inches and a standard deviation of 2.52 inches. Do the data indicate that the Australians are on the average taller than the Englishmen?
questions.a: Test H₀: μ_A = μ_E against H₁: μ_A > μ_E (Australians taller), a right-tailed test with critical value 1.645 at α = 0.05 (2.33 at 1%). The standard error of the difference is √[(2.5²/6400)+(2.52²/1600)] = √(0.0009766 + 0.003969) = √0.004946 ≈ 0.0703. Hence Z = (68.55 − 67.85)/0.0703 = 0.70/0.0703 ≈ 9.95. Since 9.95 far exceeds both 1.645 and 2.33, H₀ is decisively rejected. The data indicate that Australians are on average significantly taller than Englishmen.
steps: H₀: μ_A = μ_E and H₁: μ_A > μ_E (Australians taller, right-tailed).
Significance level α = 0.05, critical value 1.645 (at 1%, 2.33).
Z = 0.70/0.0703 ≈ 9.95; decision rule: reject H₀ if Z > 1.645, and 9.95 > 1.645 (also > 2.33).
Conclusion: H₀ is decisively rejected — Australians are on average significantly taller than Englishmen.
